d: The book's worked example: Twitter's QPS and storage, step by step
goal: Your win today: from five written assumptions you can derive ~3,500 write QPS, ~7,000 peak QPS, 30 TB of media a day and ~55 PB over five years, out loud, in under two minutes.
bookSections: 'Example: Estimate Twitter QPS and storage requirements' (assumptions, QPS, peak QPS, average tweet size, media storage, 5-year storage) and the 'Tips' items on writing down assumptions and commonly asked estimates

stages.title: Pin your assumptions
stages.sub: Write them down before any math
stages.teaches: Book tip: write down your assumptions; they're what you and the interviewer check against later. The book's assumptions (it notes these are not real Twitter numbers): 300 million monthly active users (MAU = distinct users in a month); 50% of users use Twitter daily; users post 2 tweets per day on average; 10% of tweets contain media; data is stored for 5 years. DAU (daily active users) = MAU × daily fraction. In a real interview you propose numbers and ask 'does that sound reasonable?' instead of waiting to be told.
stages.interaction: An interviewer chat bubble gives the prompt: 'Estimate Twitter's QPS and storage requirements.' Below, a deck of 8 assumption cards: the 5 real ones plus 3 distractors ('Twitter is written in Scala', 'There are 2,000 engineers', 'Tweets are sorted by time'). Learner drags/taps the cards they need onto a sticky-note board titled 'Assumptions'. Correct cards stick with a pin; distractors slide off with a one-line reason ('doesn't change QPS or storage'). When all 5 are pinned, the interviewer replies 'Sounds reasonable, go ahead', and the board stays visible (sticky) for stages 2–4.
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'Why write assumptions on the board first?' options: 'So you and the interviewer can check and adjust the math against them' (correct) / 'Because interviewers grade handwriting' / 'So you can skip asking any questions later'.

stages.title: Crunch the QPS
stages.sub: Users → tweets per day → tweets per second → peak
stages.teaches: QPS = queries per second. DAU = 300 million × 50% = 150 million. Tweets per day = 150 million × 2 = 300 million. Tweet QPS = 300 million ÷ 24 hours ÷ 3,600 seconds = 300,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 3,472 ≈ ~3,500. Peak QPS = 2 × QPS ≈ ~7,000 (the book's simple rule: traffic isn't flat, so plan for a peak; 2× is an assumption, not a law). Shortcut check: 86,400 ≈ 10^5 gives 3,000, the same order of magnitude.
stages.interaction: Calculate-and-check as a 4-step chain. Each step is a row: formula on the left with the learner's own number from the previous step carried in, an input box + unit, and a check button. Steps: DAU (150 million), tweets/day (300 million), write QPS (accept 3,000–4,000; exact 3,472), peak QPS (accept 6,000–8,000). After step 3, a 'precision' chip pops up: if the learner typed 3,472.22, it suggests 'Say ~3,500: precision isn't expected'. A side mini-tool 'seconds in a day' expands to show 24 × 3,600 = 86,400 ≈ 10^5. When done, a little animated counter shows tweets ticking in at ~3,500 per second with a peak spike to ~7,000.
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'Why compute peak QPS, not just average?' options: 'Servers must handle the busiest moments, not the average' (correct) / 'Peak QPS is what determines storage' / 'Average QPS is always exactly half of peak'.

stages.title: Weigh the storage
stages.sub: Bytes per tweet → terabytes per day → petabytes
stages.teaches: Average tweet size (book): tweet_id 64 bytes, text 140 bytes, media 1 MB. Book estimates only media, since it dominates: media storage per day = 150 million × 2 × 10% × 1 MB = 30 million media items × 1 MB = 30 TB per day. 5-year media storage = 30 TB × 365 × 5 ≈ 54,750 TB ≈ 55 PB. Sanity check on text: 300 million tweets × ~204 bytes ≈ 61 GB/day, about 500× smaller than media, which is why it's fine to ignore. Bonus (not in book): 30 TB/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 350 MB/s of incoming media, about 2.8 Gbps.
stages.interaction: Predict-then-watch, then calculate. Predict: 'Which dominates daily storage: tweet text or media?' (text / media / about equal). Then two growing stacks of disk icons animate side by side as the learner computes: left stack 'text' (inputs: tweets/day 300 million × 204 bytes → ~61 GB), right stack 'media' (150 million × 2 × 10% × 1 MB → 30 TB). The media stack visibly dwarfs text (the text stack is drawn to scale as a tiny sliver with a magnifier). Next card: '5 years' → learner enters 30 TB × 365 × 5; accept 50–60 PB (or 50,000–60,000 TB). A 'zero tally' helper from Quest 2.1 is available on tap.
stages.check: Prediction scored (correct: media). Q.quiz: 'The book's 5-year media estimate is about…' options: '55 PB' (correct) / '55 TB' / '5.5 EB'.

stages.title: Turn the knobs
stages.teaches: Book tip: commonly asked estimates are QPS, peak QPS, storage, cache, number of servers. The results scale linearly with each assumption: double DAU → double everything; double media share → double media storage; peak factor changes QPS but not storage; retention changes total storage but not daily. Things the book's example leaves out that a senior mentions: replication (stored 3 times → ~165 PB), read traffic (Twitter is read-heavy; reads are many times writes), and growth over 5 years.
stages.interaction: A live 'napkin calculator' panel with sliders: MAU (100M–1B), daily % (10–100), tweets/user/day (0.5–10), media % (0–50), media size (100 KB–10 MB), retention years (1–10), replication factor (1–5), peak multiplier (1–10). Outputs update instantly: DAU, write QPS, peak QPS, media/day, total storage. Default = book values (outputs ~3,500 / ~7,000 / 30 TB / ~55 PB). Three challenges (shown as a checklist): (1) 'Make total storage ~165 PB without changing users' → replication 3; (2) 'Double QPS by moving only one slider' → daily % to 100 or tweets/day to 4; (3) 'Find a slider that changes peak QPS but not storage' → peak multiplier. A 'reset to book' button restores defaults.
stages.check: Q.quiz: 'The interviewer says: store 3 copies of every file. Your 5-year number becomes…' options: 'About 165 PB' (correct) / 'Still about 55 PB; copies are free' / 'About 55 TB'.

stages.title: Boss: The What-If Wyvern
stages.teaches: Applies sensitivity: each assumption scales the result linearly, and some don't touch it at all.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with shared choices: '×2', '×10', '÷2', 'No change'. Each scenario names one change from the book's baseline and asks about one specific output. (1) 'DAU doubles. Write QPS?' → ×2; (2) 'Media share goes from 10% to 20%. Daily media storage?' → ×2; (3) 'Users post 1 tweet a day instead of 2. Peak QPS?' → ÷2; (4) 'Tweet text grows from 140 to 280 characters. Daily media storage?' → No change; (5) 'Peak multiplier goes from 2× to 4×. 5-year storage?' → No change; (6) 'MAU grows from 300 million to 3 billion, same daily %. Daily media storage?' → ×10; (7) 'Retention goes from 5 to 10 years. Total media storage?' → ×2. Each 'why' shows the formula with the changed factor highlighted.
stages.check: Boss HP; first-run hearts at stake.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.sub: The full Twitter estimate in 60 seconds
stages.teaches: Recall of the whole worked example.
stages.interaction: Q.drill prompt: 'Walk me through estimating Twitter's QPS and storage.' Model answer: 'Assumptions first: 300 million MAU, half use it daily, 2 tweets per user per day, 10% have media at about 1 MB, keep data 5 years. DAU is 150 million, so 300 million tweets a day. Divide by 86,400 seconds: about 3,500 tweets per second, and I'll plan for a 2× peak, about 7,000. Storage is dominated by media: 150 million × 2 × 10% × 1 MB is 30 TB a day; times 365 times 5 is about 55 PB. Text is only ~60 GB a day, so I ignore it. With 3× replication it's ~165 PB, and reads will be much higher than writes, so next I'd estimate read QPS and a cache.'
stages.check: Self-grade checks: 'Stated assumptions first', 'Got ~3,500 QPS and ~7,000 peak', 'Got 30 TB/day and ~55 PB over 5 years', 'Mentioned something the book leaves out (replication, reads, or growth)'.

caveats: The book says its numbers are for the exercise only, not Twitter's real figures.
The 2× peak rule is a simplification. Real spikes can be far larger: Twitter's 2013 record was 143,199 tweets per second against an average of about 5,700, roughly 25×.
The book's 64-byte tweet_id is generous: Twitter's Snowflake IDs are 64 bits (8 bytes). It doesn't matter because media dominates.
Text limit is 280 characters since 2017, and UTF-8 text can use up to 4 bytes per character; still tiny next to media.
The example estimates writes and media only; it ignores replication, read traffic (timelines are read far more than written), metadata/indexes, and user growth over five years.
